specStatements.text: Students should be able to describe simply how the genome and its interaction with the environment influence the development of the phenotype of an organism.

Differences in the characteristics of individuals in a population is called variation and may be due to differences in: the genes they have inherited (genetic causes); the conditions in which they have developed (environmental causes); a combination of genes and the environment.

Students should be able to: state that there is usually extensive genetic variation within a population of a species; recall that all variants arise from mutations and that: most have no effect on the phenotype; some influence phenotype; very few determine phenotype.
Mutations occur continuously. Very rarely a mutation will lead to a new phenotype. If the new phenotype is suited to an environmental change it can lead to a relatively rapid change in the species.

Students should be able to describe evolution as a change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through a process of natural selection which may result in the formation of a new species.
The theory of evolution by natural selection states that all species of living things have evolved from simple life forms that first developed more than three billion years ago.
Students should be able to explain how evolution occurs through natural selection of variants that give rise to phenotypes best suited to their environment.
If two populations of one species become so different in phenotype that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring they have formed two new species.
Students should be able to explain the impact of selective breeding of food plants and domesticated animals.

Selective breeding (artificial selection) is the process by which humans breed plants and animals for particular genetic characteristics. Humans have been doing this for thousands of years since they first bred food crops from wild plants and domesticated animals.

Selective breeding involves choosing parents with the desired characteristic from a mixed population. They are bred together. From the offspring those with the desired characteristic are bred together. This continues over many generations until all the offspring show the desired characteristic.

The characteristic can be chosen for usefulness or appearance: Disease resistance in food crops.; Animals which produce more meat or milk.; Domestic dogs with a gentle nature.; Large or unusual flowers.
Selective breeding can lead to 'inbreeding' where some breeds are particularly prone to disease or inherited defects.
Students should be able to describe genetic engineering as a process which involves modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic.
Plant crops have been genetically engineered to be resistant to diseases or to produce bigger better fruits.
Bacterial cells have been genetically engineered to produce useful substances such as human insulin to treat diabetes.
Students should be able to explain the potential benefits and risks of genetic engineering in agriculture and in medicine and that some people have objections.
In genetic engineering, genes from the chromosomes of humans and other organisms can be 'cut out' and transferred to cells of other organisms.

Crops that have had their genes modified in this way are called genetically modified (GM) crops. GM crops include ones that are resistant to insect attack or to herbicides. GM crops generally show increased yields.
Concerns about GM crops include the effect on populations of wild flowers and insects. Some people feel the effects of eating GM crops on human health have not been fully explored.
Modern medical research is exploring the possibility of genetic modification to overcome some inherited disorders.
Students should be able to describe the main steps in the process of genetic engineering.

In genetic engineering: enzymes are used to isolate the required gene; this gene is inserted into a vector, usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus; the vector is used to insert the gene into the required cells; genes are transferred to the cells of animals, plants or microorganisms at an early stage in their development so that they develop with desired characteristics.
Tissue culture: using small groups of cells from part of a plant to grow identical new plants. This is important for preserving rare plant species or commercially in nurseries.
Cuttings: an older, but simple, method used by gardeners to produce many identical new plants from a parent plant.
Embryo transplants: splitting apart cells from a developing animal embryo before they become specialised, then transplanting the identical embryos into host mothers.

Adult cell cloning: The nucleus is removed from an unfertilised egg cell.; The nucleus from an adult body cell, such as a skin cell, is inserted into the egg cell.; An electric shock stimulates the egg cell to divide to form an embryo.; These embryo cells contain the same genetic information as the adult skin cell.; When the embryo has developed into a ball of cells, it is inserted into the womb of an adult female to continue its development.

concepts.definition: The characteristics of an organism. The phenotype develops as a result of the genome of the organism and its interaction with the environment.

Differences in the characteristics of individuals in a population. Variation may be due to the genes they have inherited (genetic causes), the conditions in which they have developed (environmental causes), or a combination of genes and the environment.

A change in the DNA of an organism. All variants arise from mutations, and mutations occur continuously. Very rarely a mutation will lead to a new phenotype, and if that new phenotype is suited to an environmental change it can lead to a relatively rapid change in the species.

concepts.term: Effect of mutations on the phenotype
concepts.definition: There is usually extensive genetic variation within a population of a species. Of the variants that arise from mutations, most have no effect on the phenotype, some influence phenotype and very few determine phenotype.
A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through a process of natural selection, which may result in the formation of a new species.

The process by which variants that give rise to phenotypes best suited to their environment are the most likely to survive and to breed successfully, so that the genes for these characteristics are passed on to the next generation.

concepts.term: Theory of evolution by natural selection
concepts.definition: The theory that all species of living things have evolved from simple life forms that first developed more than three billion years ago.
Two populations of one species have formed two new species when they become so different in phenotype that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

The process by which humans breed plants and animals for particular genetic characteristics. Parents with the desired characteristic are chosen from a mixed population and bred together; from the offspring, those with the desired characteristic are bred together, and this continues over many generations until all the offspring show the desired characteristic. Humans have done this for thousands of years, since they first bred food crops from wild plants and domesticated animals.

The characteristic that humans select for in selective breeding, chosen for usefulness or appearance. Examples are disease resistance in food crops, animals which produce more meat or milk, domestic dogs with a gentle nature, and large or unusual flowers.
Breeding from closely related individuals, which selective breeding can lead to. Some breeds produced in this way are particularly prone to disease or inherited defects.

A process which involves modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic. Genes from the chromosomes of humans and other organisms can be 'cut out' and transferred to cells of other organisms.

Crops that have had their genes modified by genetic engineering. GM crops include ones that are resistant to insect attack or to herbicides, and GM crops generally show increased yields. Plant crops have also been genetically engineered to be resistant to diseases or to produce bigger better fruits. Concerns about GM crops include the effect on populations of wild flowers and insects, and some people feel that the effects of eating GM crops on human health have not been fully explored.
Bacterial cells that have been genetically engineered to produce useful substances, such as human insulin to treat diabetes.
Modern medical research is exploring the possibility of genetic modification to overcome some inherited disorders.

In genetic engineering, the structure that carries the required gene into cells, usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus. Enzymes are used to isolate the required gene, the gene is inserted into the vector, and the vector is used to insert the gene into the required cells. Genes are transferred to the cells of animals, plants or microorganisms at an early stage in their development so that they develop with the desired characteristics.
Using small groups of cells from part of a plant to grow identical new plants. This is important for preserving rare plant species or commercially in nurseries.
An older, but simple, method used by gardeners to produce many identical new plants from a parent plant.
Splitting apart cells from a developing animal embryo before they become specialised, then transplanting the identical embryos into host mothers.

A process in which the nucleus is removed from an unfertilised egg cell and the nucleus from an adult body cell, such as a skin cell, is inserted into the egg cell. An electric shock stimulates the egg cell to divide to form an embryo, and these embryo cells contain the same genetic information as the adult skin cell. When the embryo has developed into a ball of cells it is inserted into the womb of an adult female to continue its development.

misconceptions.question: Tomato plants grown from cuttings of one parent plant are kept in different amounts of light and grow to different heights. What has caused the difference?
misconceptions.correct: The conditions in which the plants developed, an environmental cause of variation.
misconceptions.misconception: Any difference in the characteristics of individuals must be due to the different genes they have inherited.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Inheritance is taught before variation, and characteristics are described as being 'passed on', so students treat genes as the only possible source of a difference and overlook the conditions in which an organism developed.
misconceptions.correction: Variation may be due to the genes they have inherited (genetic causes), the conditions in which they have developed (environmental causes), or a combination of genes and the environment; the genome and its interaction with the environment influence the development of the phenotype.

misconceptions.question: A mutation occurs in an organism. What is the most likely effect on its phenotype?
misconceptions.correct: There is no effect on the phenotype.
misconceptions.misconception: Every mutation produces a change in the phenotype of the organism.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mutations are usually introduced through striking examples in which an organism is visibly changed, so students assume that any change in the DNA must show up in the organism.
misconceptions.correction: All variants arise from mutations, but most have no effect on the phenotype, some influence phenotype and very few determine phenotype.

misconceptions.question: Why do mutations occur in a population?
misconceptions.correct: Mutations occur continuously, whatever the environment is like.
misconceptions.misconception: Mutations are produced by a change in the environment, because the organisms then need a new phenotype.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Examples always pair a new phenotype with an environmental change, so students read the environmental change as the cause of the mutation rather than as the thing that makes the new phenotype useful.
misconceptions.correction: Mutations occur continuously. Very rarely a mutation will lead to a new phenotype, and if the new phenotype is suited to an environmental change it can lead to a relatively rapid change in the species.

misconceptions.question: What does it mean to say that a population has evolved?
misconceptions.correct: The inherited characteristics of the population have changed over time.
misconceptions.misconception: An individual organism evolves during its own lifetime.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech 'evolve' simply means 'gradually change', so students picture one animal changing rather than the inherited characteristics of a whole population changing across generations.
misconceptions.correction: Evolution is a change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through a process of natural selection which may result in the formation of a new species.

misconceptions.question: How does a population come to be better suited to its environment?
misconceptions.correct: Variants already present that give the phenotypes best suited to the environment survive and breed.
misconceptions.misconception: Organisms develop the characteristics that they need in order to survive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Purpose-driven language such as 'the animal needed a thicker coat' is common in everyday explanations, and it is easier to imagine an organism responding to a problem than to imagine that variation was already there.
misconceptions.correction: Evolution occurs through natural selection of variants that give rise to phenotypes best suited to their environment, and all variants arise from mutations, which occur continuously.

misconceptions.question: Two separated populations of one species now look very different. Are they two species?
misconceptions.correct: Only if they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
misconceptions.misconception: Two populations are separate species once they look different enough to be told apart.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Species are usually met as named pictures in a key, so appearance becomes the test students apply, and the breeding test is rarely used in earlier work.
misconceptions.correction: If two populations of one species become so different in phenotype that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring they have formed two new species.

misconceptions.question: Who decides which individuals are bred together in selective breeding?
misconceptions.correct: Humans choose the parents that have the desired characteristic.
misconceptions.misconception: Selective breeding happens on its own in a population, in the same way as natural selection.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Natural selection and selective breeding are taught together and both end with a population showing a characteristic, so the human choice of parents is forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: Selective breeding (artificial selection) is the process by which humans breed plants and animals for particular genetic characteristics, choosing parents with the desired characteristic from a mixed population.

misconceptions.question: How long does selective breeding take before all the offspring show the desired characteristic?
misconceptions.correct: Many generations of choosing and breeding.
misconceptions.misconception: Breeding the two chosen parents once produces offspring that all show the desired characteristic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Written answers often describe a single round of breeding, and students forget that the offspring still vary so the choosing and breeding has to be repeated.
misconceptions.correction: From the offspring those with the desired characteristic are bred together. This continues over many generations until all the offspring show the desired characteristic.

misconceptions.question: Give one problem that selective breeding can cause.
misconceptions.correct: It can lead to inbreeding, so some breeds are particularly prone to disease or inherited defects.
misconceptions.misconception: Selective breeding can only improve a breed, because breeders keep the best individuals and breed out the harmful characteristics.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Selective breeding is introduced through its successes, such as more milk, more meat and disease resistance in crops, so students assume the process removes anything harmful.
misconceptions.correction: Selective breeding can lead to 'inbreeding' where some breeds are particularly prone to disease or inherited defects.

misconceptions.question: What makes genetic engineering different from selective breeding?
misconceptions.correct: A gene from another organism is introduced into the genome of the organism.
misconceptions.misconception: Genetic engineering is just a quicker form of selective breeding, in which the best parents are chosen and bred.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both processes are presented as ways of obtaining a desired characteristic, and 'engineering the genes' sounds to students like choosing which genes are passed on.
misconceptions.correction: Genetic engineering is a process which involves modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic.

misconceptions.question: How does genetic engineering differ from cloning a plant by tissue culture?
misconceptions.correct: Genetic engineering introduces a gene from another organism, while tissue culture grows identical new plants from small groups of cells.
misconceptions.misconception: Genetic engineering and cloning are the same thing, because both are laboratory ways of making new organisms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both processes appear in the same part of the course and both are pictured as laboratory work on cells, so students merge them into one idea of 'making organisms artificially'.
misconceptions.correction: Genetic engineering modifies the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism, whereas tissue culture uses small groups of cells from part of a plant to grow identical new plants.

misconceptions.question: How is genetic modification used at present for inherited disorders?
misconceptions.correct: Modern medical research is exploring the possibility of using it to overcome some inherited disorders.
misconceptions.misconception: Genetic modification is already a routine treatment that cures inherited disorders in patients.
misconceptions.whyItArises: News reports about changing genes describe cures, and students do not separate research that is exploring a possibility from treatment that is in routine use.
misconceptions.correction: Modern medical research is exploring the possibility of genetic modification to overcome some inherited disorders.

misconceptions.question: Give one concern that some people have about GM crops.
misconceptions.correct: The effect on populations of wild flowers and insects.
misconceptions.misconception: People object to GM crops because GM crops give lower yields than other crops.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that GM crops are controversial and assume the objection must be that they do not work, rather than a concern about wild populations or about human health.
misconceptions.correction: GM crops generally show increased yields. Concerns about GM crops include the effect on populations of wild flowers and insects, and some people feel the effects of eating GM crops on human health have not been fully explored.

misconceptions.question: How does the required gene get into the cells of the organism being engineered?
misconceptions.correct: It is inserted into a vector, usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus, and the vector inserts it into the required cells.
misconceptions.misconception: The enzymes that cut out the required gene also carry it into the cells, so no vector is needed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Enzymes are the first thing named in the process and are remembered as 'the tool that does the job', so the separate vector step is left out.
misconceptions.correction: Enzymes are used to isolate the required gene; this gene is inserted into a vector, usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus; the vector is used to insert the gene into the required cells.

misconceptions.question: How do plants grown from cuttings or by tissue culture compare with the parent plant?
misconceptions.correct: They are identical to the parent plant.
misconceptions.misconception: Plants grown from cuttings or by tissue culture show variation from the parent, as any offspring do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn early that offspring differ from their parents, and they apply that rule to cloning as well as to reproduction involving two parents.
misconceptions.correction: Tissue culture uses small groups of cells from part of a plant to grow identical new plants, and cuttings are used to produce many identical new plants from a parent plant.

misconceptions.question: In adult cell cloning, where does the genetic information of the embryo come from?
misconceptions.correct: From the nucleus of the adult body cell that was inserted into the egg cell.
misconceptions.misconception: The genetic information comes from the unfertilised egg cell that the embryo grows from.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The egg cell is the visible starting point of the process, and students forget that its nucleus is removed before the nucleus from the adult body cell is inserted.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus is removed from an unfertilised egg cell and the nucleus from an adult body cell, such as a skin cell, is inserted into the egg cell; these embryo cells contain the same genetic information as the adult skin cell.

mcqs.stem: Two plants grown from cuttings of the same parent plant are given different amounts of light. One grows much taller than the other. What does this difference show?

options.text: The plants inherited different genes for their height
options.rationale: A student who believes every difference must be genetic picks this, but the plants were grown from cuttings of one parent plant, so the difference here has an environmental cause.

options.text: The change in light has caused a mutation in one plant
options.rationale: A student who thinks the environment produces mutations to order picks this, but mutations occur continuously and a difference in growing conditions is an environmental cause of variation, not a mutation.

options.text: The environment has influenced the phenotype of the plants
options.rationale: The genome and its interaction with the environment influence the development of the phenotype, so the different light conditions have produced different heights.

options.text: One plant has evolved to be taller in the brighter light
options.rationale: A student who thinks an individual evolves in its lifetime picks this, but evolution is a change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time, not a change in one plant.

mcqs.stem: Which of these describes the causes of variation between individuals in a population?

options.text: Inherited genes, the conditions of development, or both
options.rationale: Variation may be due to the genes they have inherited, the conditions in which they have developed, or a combination of genes and the environment.

options.text: Inherited genes alone, which are passed on by the parents
options.rationale: A student who believes all differences are genetic picks this, but the conditions in which individuals have developed are also a cause of variation.

options.text: Mutations that are produced by a change in the environment
options.rationale: A student who thinks the environment produces mutations picks this, but mutations occur continuously and are not made to order by an environmental change.

options.text: Mutations alone, because every one changes the phenotype
options.rationale: A student who thinks every mutation changes the phenotype picks this, but most mutations have no effect on the phenotype and variation also has environmental causes.

mcqs.stem: All variants arise from mutations. Which statement about mutations and phenotype is correct?

options.text: Most mutations lead to a change in the phenotype
options.rationale: A student who thinks a change in DNA must show in the organism picks this, but most mutations have no effect on the phenotype.

options.text: Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype
options.rationale: Most variants have no effect on the phenotype, some influence phenotype and very few determine phenotype.

options.text: Mutations happen only when the environment changes
options.rationale: A student who thinks mutations are produced by environmental change picks this, but mutations occur continuously.

options.text: Mutations build up in an organism during its life
options.rationale: A student who thinks individuals change and evolve during their lifetime picks this, but the point at issue is the effect of mutations on the phenotype, and most have no effect at all.

mcqs.stem: A mutation produces a new phenotype in a population. The environment then changes, and the new phenotype is suited to the new conditions. What is the likely result?

options.text: More mutations of the same type occur in the population
options.rationale: A student who thinks environmental change produces mutations picks this, but mutations occur continuously and are not increased to suit new conditions.

options.text: A relatively rapid change in the species can take place
options.rationale: If the new phenotype is suited to an environmental change it can lead to a relatively rapid change in the species.

options.text: Each organism changes to the new phenotype in its lifetime
options.rationale: A student who thinks individuals evolve during their lifetime picks this, but the change occurs across a population over generations, not within one organism.

options.text: The organisms develop the new phenotype that they need
options.rationale: A student who thinks organisms develop the features they need picks this, but the variant arose from a mutation before the environment changed.

options.text: A change in the characteristics of an animal in its lifetime
options.rationale: A student who thinks individuals evolve picks this, but evolution is a change in a population over time, not a change in one organism.

options.text: A change in the inherited characteristics of a population
options.rationale: Evolution is a change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through a process of natural selection.

options.text: A change in appearance that makes a population a new species
options.rationale: A student who thinks a change in appearance alone makes a new species picks this, but a new species is formed only when the populations can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

options.text: The growth of the characteristics that organisms need most
options.rationale: A student who thinks organisms develop the features they need picks this, but evolution acts on variants that already arose from mutations.

mcqs.stem: In a beetle population most beetles are pale and a few are dark. The tree bark the beetles live on becomes darker, so birds find the pale beetles more easily. After many generations most of the beetles are dark. Which statement explains this?

options.text: The beetles developed a dark colour because they needed it
options.rationale: A student who thinks organisms develop the features they need picks this, but the dark variant was already present in the population before the bark changed.

options.text: Each pale beetle became darker as the tree bark got darker
options.rationale: A student who thinks individuals evolve in their lifetime picks this, but the inherited characteristics of the population changed across generations.

options.text: The darker bark caused the mutations that made beetles darker
options.rationale: A student who thinks the environment produces mutations picks this, but mutations occur continuously and the darker bark only made the existing dark variant better suited.

options.text: Dark beetles survived to breed and passed on their variant
options.rationale: Natural selection acts on variants that give rise to phenotypes best suited to their environment, and those beetles pass the genes on to the next generation.

mcqs.stem: Two populations of one species have been separated for a very long time and now look very different. What must be shown before they are classed as two new species?

options.text: That their phenotypes are different enough to tell apart
options.rationale: A student who uses appearance as the test picks this, but two populations may look different and still interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

options.text: That each population has developed the features that it needs
options.rationale: A student who thinks organisms develop the features they need picks this, but the test for a new species is whether fertile offspring can be produced.

options.text: That the individuals have changed during their own lifetimes
options.rationale: A student who thinks individuals evolve picks this, but only inherited characteristics of the populations are relevant to the formation of a new species.

options.text: That they can no longer produce fertile offspring together
options.rationale: Two new species have formed when the populations are so different in phenotype that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

mcqs.stem: A farmer chooses the cows that produce the most milk and breeds them together. From their offspring he again breeds those that produce the most milk, and he repeats this for many generations. Which statement about this process is correct?

options.text: It is natural selection, as the best cows survive and breed
options.rationale: A student who thinks selective breeding happens on its own picks this, but here the farmer chooses which parents are bred together.

options.text: It is genetic engineering, as the genome is being modified
options.rationale: A student who confuses the two processes picks this, but no gene from another organism has been introduced into the genome.

options.text: It is selective breeding, as the farmer chose the parents
options.rationale: Selective breeding is the process by which humans breed animals for particular genetic characteristics, here the useful characteristic of producing more milk.

options.text: It was complete once the first chosen cows had been bred
options.rationale: A student who thinks one round of breeding is enough picks this, but the choosing and breeding continues over many generations until all the offspring show the desired characteristic.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about selective breeding is correct?

options.text: It removes inherited defects from the breeds produced
options.rationale: A student who thinks selective breeding can only improve a breed picks this, but it can lead to inbreeding, and some breeds are then prone to inherited defects.

options.text: It happens in wild populations with no human choice
options.rationale: A student who confuses it with natural selection picks this, but humans choose the parents with the desired characteristic.

options.text: It can lead to inbreeding in the breeds it produces
options.rationale: Selective breeding can lead to 'inbreeding' where some breeds are particularly prone to disease or inherited defects.

options.text: It adds a gene from another organism to the offspring
options.rationale: A student who confuses it with genetic engineering picks this, but selective breeding only breeds together parents that already have the characteristic.

options.text: A gene is transferred to the cells of another organism
options.rationale: Genes from the chromosomes of humans and other organisms can be 'cut out' and transferred to cells of other organisms, modifying the genome.

options.text: Parents with the desired characteristic are bred together
options.rationale: A student who treats genetic engineering as fast selective breeding picks this, but no gene is introduced from another organism when parents are bred.

options.text: Cells from one organism are grown into identical copies
options.rationale: A student who merges genetic engineering with cloning picks this, but growing identical copies from cells is tissue culture, and the genome is not modified.

options.text: A faulty gene in a patient is replaced to cure a disorder
options.rationale: A student who thinks inherited disorders are already cured this way picks this, but modern medical research is still exploring that possibility.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the uses of genetic engineering is correct?

options.text: Bacterial cells have been engineered to make human insulin
options.rationale: Bacterial cells have been genetically engineered to produce useful substances such as human insulin to treat diabetes.

options.text: Tissue culture is used to insert genes in bacterial cells
options.rationale: A student who merges cloning with genetic engineering picks this, but tissue culture grows identical new plants and does not add genes.

options.text: Inherited disorders are now cured using genetic modification
options.rationale: A student who has read of gene cures picks this, but modern medical research is exploring the possibility of genetic modification to overcome some inherited disorders.

options.text: Crops are engineered by breeding the best plants together
options.rationale: A student who confuses genetic engineering with selective breeding picks this, but engineering a crop means introducing a gene from another organism.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about genetically modified (GM) crops is correct?

options.text: GM crops generally produce lower yields than other food crops
options.rationale: A student who assumes the objection is that GM crops do not work picks this, but GM crops generally show increased yields.

options.text: GM crops are grown from cells taken from one parent plant
options.rationale: A student who merges genetic engineering with cloning picks this, but a GM crop has had its genes modified by introducing a gene from another organism.

options.text: GM crops may affect populations of wild flowers and insects
options.rationale: Concerns about GM crops include the effect on populations of wild flowers and insects, and some people feel the effects on human health have not been fully explored.

options.text: GM crops are used to cure inherited disorders in patients
options.rationale: A student who confuses agricultural and medical uses picks this, but genetic modification to overcome inherited disorders is still being explored by research.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the main steps in the process of genetic engineering?

options.text: Enzymes isolate the gene, which a vector puts into cells
options.rationale: Enzymes are used to isolate the required gene, this gene is inserted into a vector, usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus, and the vector is used to insert the gene into the required cells at an early stage of their development.

options.text: Enzymes cut out the gene and carry it into the cells
options.rationale: A student who remembers only the enzymes picks this, but the isolated gene must be inserted into a vector, which then inserts it into the required cells.

options.text: Cells are taken from an organism and grown into copies
options.rationale: A student who merges genetic engineering with cloning picks this, but growing copies of cells does not isolate or transfer a gene.

options.text: The best parent organisms are bred to combine genes
options.rationale: A student who treats genetic engineering as selective breeding picks this, but the required gene is isolated by enzymes and carried into cells by a vector.

mcqs.stem: A nursery needs many new plants that are identical to one rare parent plant. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A gene from another plant would give identical copies
options.rationale: A student who merges genetic engineering with cloning picks this, but adding a gene modifies the genome instead of copying the parent plant.

options.text: Tissue culture of the parent's cells gives identical plants
options.rationale: Tissue culture uses small groups of cells from part of a plant to grow identical new plants, which is important for preserving rare plant species.

options.text: Cuttings from the parent give plants showing variation
options.rationale: A student who expects offspring to vary picks this, but cuttings are used to produce many identical new plants from a parent plant.

options.text: One generation of breeding would give identical offspring
options.rationale: A student who thinks one round of breeding fixes a characteristic picks this, but breeding produces offspring that vary, so it cannot give identical plants.

mcqs.stem: In adult cell cloning the nucleus is removed from an unfertilised egg cell, the nucleus from an adult skin cell is inserted, and an electric shock makes the egg cell divide to form an embryo. What are the embryo cells like?

options.text: They have the genetic information of the egg donor
options.rationale: A student who treats the egg cell as the source of the genetic information picks this, but the nucleus of the egg cell was removed first.

options.text: They have genetic information varying from the adult
options.rationale: A student who expects offspring to vary picks this, but the embryo cells are clones of the adult body cell.

options.text: They have an extra gene added from another organism
options.rationale: A student who merges cloning with genetic engineering picks this, but no gene from another organism is introduced in adult cell cloning.

options.text: They have the same genetic information as the skin cell
options.rationale: These embryo cells contain the same genetic information as the adult skin cell whose nucleus was inserted into the egg cell.
